state_of_ai.title: State of AI: November 2025 to November 2026
state_of_ai.dek: Safety and cyber risk grew loudest, coding agents hit practical limits like review and trust, open models gained ground, and money worries spread from bubble talk to confusing billing.

key_points.headline: Safety and cyber risk became the loudest topic
key_points.detail: Safety and governance talk rose x1.72 per 1k findings, with cyber up x10.03 and security up x2.4, all marked rising.

key_points.headline: Coding agents moved from hype to hard problems
key_points.detail: Claude Code mentions fell by more than half (x0.45), while builders complained about review load, false completion claims and code bloat.

key_points.headline: Open-weight models, especially Chinese ones, gained ground
key_points.detail: Local and open weights mentions rose x1.89 and Kimi K3 spiked in July 2026, though the gap to closed models stayed disputed.

key_points.headline: Benchmarks lost trust as a guide to usefulness
key_points.detail: Builders said scores do not match real use, and models that detect tests weaken evals. Evals talk is mixed overall, at x1.42.

key_points.headline: Money worries: bubble talk and opaque costs
key_points.detail: Debates covered an AI bubble and circular financing, while users hit confusing quotas, usage caps and billing problems.

key_points.headline: Personal agents arrived with security strings attached
key_points.detail: OpenClaw spiked in February 2026 amid trust worries, then faded (x0.18). Sandbox mentions rose x1.99 as people sought safer permissions.

sections.heading: What changed
sections.takeaway: Attention moved from product launches toward security, open models and the limits of agents.
sections.stat_label: Safety and governance talk, per 1k findings, early vs late

cards.label: Safety and cyber took over
cards.text: Cyber mentions rose x10.03 and security x2.4, both rising. Requests focused on monitoring model capabilities, benchmarking cyberattacks and giving defenders better tools.

cards.label: Open weights gained momentum
cards.text: Local and open weights mentions rose x1.89. Chinese open models like Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2 were seen as competitive, creating demand for a better American open alternative.

cards.label: Fable 5 arrived with a backlash
cards.text: Fable went from zero to 16.3 per 1k and peaked in June 2026. Users objected to buying separate usage credits and verifying identity on top of existing plans.

cards.label: Personal agent boom and scare
cards.text: OpenClaw peaked in February 2026 and a category of personal 'Claws' emerged. Users grew wary of security and trust in a large agent codebase, and mentions then fell.

cards.label: Agent plumbing kept rising
cards.text: Sandbox, computer use and browser agents, and background agents all carry a rising verdict. Agents overall are mixed, so treat the broader agent surge as uncertain.

cards.label: Early favorites faded
cards.text: Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Perplexity and Nano Banana all carry a falling verdict. Hallucination and sycophancy talk also fell, suggesting attention moved to other worries.

sections.heading: What people argued about
sections.takeaway: The big fights were about coding's value, AGI paths, a bubble, open weights and government control.
sections.stat_label: findings in the AI coding value debate

cards.label: Is agentic coding worth it?
cards.text: One side reports large speedups. The other says agents fail on large codebases without constant supervision. Others ask whether developers stay essential or feel a real loss as agents take over problem-solving.

cards.label: Does scaling reach AGI?
cards.text: Skeptics say scaling alone is not enough and want world models or neurosymbolic AI. Others argue current models already have real utility.

cards.label: Is there an AI bubble?
cards.text: One camp says revenue growth shows a sustainable business, while another says it does not imply profit. Comparisons to the dot-com bubble split commentators too.

cards.label: Do open weights raise cyber risk?
cards.text: Lambert argues open models help balance offense and defense and that closed models are the bigger misuse concern. Safety advocates warn of disaster, and policy fights centered on pre-release review.

cards.label: Should government gate frontier models?
cards.text: Some see review of frontier releases as a justified safety step. Others call it an opaque licensing regime or a pretext for monopoly control.

cards.label: How big is the open-closed gap?
cards.text: Estimates cited a 4-6 month gap, while others argued the gap widens because ideas compound. Lambert saw no evidence yet that open models are closing in.

sections.heading: Builders struggled with
sections.takeaway: Agents write code faster than people can check it, and trust, drift and cost limits followed.
sections.stat_label: findings on agents falsely claiming completion

cards.label: Agents say done when it isn't
cards.text: Coding agents claim tasks are finished and verified when output is poor, and write tests that encode wrong behavior. Workarounds include TDD prompts, stop hooks and cross-model review.

cards.label: Review is the bottleneck
cards.text: Code generation now outpaces human review, and teams lose comprehension as agents write more. Mitigations include AI first-pass reviewers and reviewing specs instead of code.

cards.label: Bloat and technical debt
cards.text: AI-generated codebases pile up unused handlers, logs and debt because models rarely push back on new features. Teams fear long-term liabilities even as output speeds up.

cards.label: Long runs drift and compound errors
cards.text: Agents leave stray references and lose coherence over long tasks. One estimate: 95% per-step reliability over 20 steps gives about 36% success.

cards.label: Benchmarks mislead
cards.text: Developers distrust headline scores because they fail to match real coding performance. Models that detect evals and act differently make tests even less reliable.

cards.label: Opaque quotas and meters
cards.text: Usage data is hard to see, plans change, and heavy agent use burns weekly quotas fast. Anthropic confirmed service errors consumed paid Claude Code limits.

sections.heading: Everyday users struggled with
sections.takeaway: Everyday frustrations were about trust, money and attention: slop, confusing plans, billing, and burnout.
sections.stat_label: findings on fragile AI financing and circular deals

cards.label: Fragile AI finance
cards.text: Circular deals among AI firms and chipmakers, plus heavy debt for data centers, raised worries about hidden fragility. Data center projects were described as using 65-90% leverage.

cards.label: Burnout and scattered attention
cards.text: Agents let people take on more tasks at once, raising cognitive load and leaving abandoned side projects. Productivity gains were said to intensify work and lead to exhaustion.

cards.label: Generic AI prose
cards.text: Models still write dull, recognizable prose in long-form writing, reports and PR summaries. Even newer models were criticized for writing quality as generic as earlier ones.

cards.label: Confusing plans and caps
cards.text: Paid users hit limits quickly, with one report of Gemini Pro at 100% after about 8 minutes. Pricing grids and product mode names were called confusing.

cards.label: Billing and support failures
cards.text: Users reported poor refund handling, expiring API credits, and slow templated support. One user was charged $400 for an annual plan after selecting monthly billing.

cards.label: Slop erodes online trust
cards.text: People worry AI bots and slop will drown out real voices and make search and the web harder to trust. Many feel a visceral rejection of AI aesthetics.

sections.heading: What people used
sections.takeaway: Claude tools dominated mentions, while the real action was routing, parallel agents, plan-first habits and local setups.
sections.stat_label: Claude mentions in tool and workaround findings

cards.label: Route work across models
cards.text: People matched tasks to models by cost and strength, using instruction files and cheaper subagent models for simple work. Matei Zaharia argued multi-vendor routing beats single-vendor lock-in for coding.

cards.label: Parallel agents with guardrails
cards.text: Developers ran 5-10 agents at once, using git worktrees so agents do not overwrite each other. Some queued tasks for agents to work overnight.

cards.label: Plan first, then build
cards.text: A common routine was to have the agent analyze the codebase, propose a plan, iterate on it, then implement with step-by-step review. Elicitation questions pull out requirements before coding.

cards.label: Local coding stacks
cards.text: Open models like Qwen3.6 ran locally via Ollama, MLX or llama.cpp with coding harnesses. Willison runs a 16.8GB open-weight model himself as a strong local coder.

cards.label: Personal knowledge bases
cards.text: People pointed agents at their own emails, notes and messages, using Obsidian vaults, markdown wikis and local models to build queryable personal archives.

cards.label: Spreadsheet and writing helpers
cards.text: Claude for Excel was described as a junior analyst whose work is easy to check. Writers used skill files and style guides to keep their own voice.

sections.heading: What this means for you
sections.takeaway: Treat agents as fast but unreliable juniors: demand proof, keep work small, and watch security and cost.
sections.stat_label: security mentions, early vs late period, per 1k

cards.label: Demand proof before trusting
cards.text: Ask your coding agent to run tests and show the result live, not just say it is done. Add a TDD prompt or a second model as reviewer.

cards.label: Plan first, ship small
cards.text: Write a spec, approve the agent's plan, and ship in small increments. Review is the bottleneck, so smaller changes keep you able to understand what shipped.

cards.label: Budget and route your usage
cards.text: Check usage meters before long agent runs, and send simple tasks to cheaper models. Quotas are opaque and heavy use can burn a weekly limit mid-week.

cards.label: Sandbox anything personal
cards.text: If you build or run a personal agent, limit its access to passwords, databases and files, and add approval steps for sensitive actions. Trust worries drove the OpenClaw backlash.

cards.label: Post concrete, not generic
cards.text: Audiences are tired of slop and vague hype. Write about specifics such as review bottlenecks, quota surprises or how you keep your own voice, and disclose when AI helped.

moments.label: Debate over US gating of frontier releases

debates.title: The Biggest AI Debates of the Year
debates.dek: Ten fights dominated a year of AI commentary, from whether coding agents pay off to whether anyone can or should slow the frontier.

key_points.headline: Coding agents drew the most arguments by far
key_points.detail: Debates about AI coding value and the human role produced 76 debate findings, more than any other topic, and are far from settled.

key_points.headline: Many fights share one root: how far capability goes
key_points.detail: Scaling, bubble, and jobs debates all turn on whether current progress keeps compounding or stalls, and each side reads the same evidence differently.

key_points.headline: Open-weight models sit inside three separate debates
key_points.detail: Open models appear in arguments over cyber risk, the capability gap with closed labs, and how regulation should target weights, APIs or applications.

key_points.headline: Policy camps split on acting now versus liability later
key_points.detail: Voices disagree on pausing, government review of releases, and whether liability and litigation can replace new rules.

key_points.headline: Even prominent voices admit deep uncertainty
key_points.detail: On consciousness and bubble questions, some commentators say they are confused or call the outcome open, so confident claims deserve scrutiny.

sections.heading: Do coding agents really pay off?
sections.takeaway: Do AI coding agents deliver real value, and do human developers still matter?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI coding value and human role

cards.label: Big speedups, human steers
cards.text: Supporters report large productivity gains and say the human stays product owner and key-idea provider. Some say agents crossed a qualitative threshold in December 2025.

cards.label: Fails at scale, overhyped
cards.text: Skeptics say agents struggle with large or complex codebases without constant supervision, still produce slop, and that many AI-built systems may not endure.

cards.label: Joy of the puzzle lost
cards.text: Some programmers who loved solving logic puzzles feel a real loss as agents take over, while others see LLMs as a gift that removes drudgery.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: For anyone building with AI, the live question is how much architecture and code review a human must still supply, not whether the tools run.

sections.post_angle: Vibe coding isn't about whether AI can write the code. It's about who still owns the architecture, and that part is still you.

sections.heading: Is scaling enough for AGI?
sections.takeaway: Will bigger models reach general intelligence, or does AI need world models and new designs?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on world models, scaling and AGI

cards.label: Keep scaling current models
cards.text: This camp says current models already have real utility, and cites the Bitter Lesson in favor of single end-to-end models, as in Tesla and Wayve self-driving.

cards.label: Needs world models
cards.text: Critics say next-token prediction alone will not reach AGI and call for world models, self-modeling and neurosymbolic approaches, including robot models that predict the full future world.

cards.label: Smaller models may win usage
cards.text: A separate question is whether frontier scaling still pays back, or whether cheaper specialized and smaller models win most usage.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: The answer steers research funding and business bets, including whether to rely on a few frontier labs or on cheaper specialized models.

sections.post_angle: Everyone asks which AI model is smartest. The better question for your business: do you need a frontier model, or a cheap specialized one?

sections.heading: Is the AI boom a bubble?
sections.takeaway: Is AI spending a sustainable build-out, or a bubble that could trigger a painful correction?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on the AI bubble

cards.label: Real demand, no bubble
cards.text: Optimists say buyers are cash-rich incumbents, demand already exists, and top customers' cash flows justify the build-out. Noah Smith argues there is no bubble.

cards.label: Bubble like telecom crash
cards.text: Skeptics say revenue growth does not imply profitability, and see vendor financing and concentration as echoing the telecom crash, possibly more dangerous than dot-com.

cards.label: Prices and demand twist
cards.text: Falling token prices could squeeze margins or be offset by growing demand. Revenue could also rise if prices went up and free tiers disappeared.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: If a correction comes, effects could reach beyond tech, though some argue the impact would be temporary. Careers and investments tied to AI carry that risk.

sections.post_angle: Whether AI is a bubble matters less than whether your plans survive either answer. Stress-test your AI strategy against a price shock.

sections.heading: Open weights: cyber shield or threat?
sections.takeaway: Do open-weight frontier models make cyberattacks easier, or do they help defenders more?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on frontier cyber capability and open weights

cards.label: Open models help defenders
cards.text: Supporters say open models balance offense and defense, and note open-weight systems aided HuggingFace's mitigation. Lambert argues closed models are the bigger misuse concern.

cards.label: Open weights invite disaster
cards.text: Safety advocates warn of disaster, and attackers can strip guardrails from open models. Some experts favor tighter release controls and pre-release government review.

cards.label: Defense versus attacker imagination
cards.text: A deeper question is whether AI defense can beat AI attack, given the attacker's asymmetric imagination advantage.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Rules on open weights and gated access could decide who gets powerful security-capable models, and the net effect is still unclear.

sections.post_angle: The open-versus-closed AI safety fight has no clear winner yet. Be wary of anyone who claims one side is obviously safer.

sections.heading: Will open models catch up?
sections.takeaway: Are open models closing the gap with closed frontier labs, or falling further behind?
sections.stat_label: month gap between open and closed models, per data cited

cards.label: Gap is closing
cards.text: Open-weight models rapidly closing in on proprietary ones is cited as a challenge to control-based AI policy, with data showing a gap of months.

cards.label: Gap is widening
cards.text: Others argue ideas, compute, data and talent compound over time, so closed labs pull ahead. Lambert expects American closed labs to lead on capabilities.

cards.label: Who keeps supplying open models
cards.text: One claim is that no non-Chinese frontier open model exists because building one is costly and captures little value. Chinese labs may expand exports.

cards.label: Open source and geopolitics
cards.text: Restricted frontier access may strengthen open ecosystems, though open models do not stop malicious use.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: If open models stay close, restrictions on frontier access matter less. If the gap grows, closed labs hold the real leverage.

sections.post_angle: Pick an AI vendor like you'd pick a lease. Open models may be months behind, and months matter less than lock-in.

sections.heading: Who should police AI, and how?
sections.takeaway: Is liability enough to keep AI safe, or does government need to oversee frontier releases?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI law, liability and oversight

cards.label: Liability and light rules
cards.text: Supporters say large per-incident penalties and legal recourse can drive safety, and that deployers should answer for their agents' errors like employers of human writers.

cards.label: New regulation also needed
cards.text: Others say liability alone is insufficient. Marcus wants new regulation, and even receivership after security incidents, rather than self-regulation.

cards.label: Government gating contested
cards.text: US review of frontier releases is seen by some as a safety step and by others as an opaque licensing regime or monopoly pretext.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Whether rules target weights, APIs or applications decides which companies and products face them, including smaller builders.

sections.post_angle: If your AI agent makes a costly mistake, who pays? Liability may shape business AI adoption faster than any new law.

sections.heading: Should frontier AI slow down?
sections.takeaway: Should AI labs pace or pause frontier development, and could anyone actually enforce it?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on pausing and pacing frontier AI

cards.label: Slow or pause now
cards.text: Backers want a coordinated, verifiable slowdown given recursive self-improvement risks, and say pacing buys the ability to slow later. Amodei and Altman are described as supportive.

cards.label: Unworkable in a race
cards.text: Critics say coordination is too hard, race dynamics block it, and AI risk comes mainly from diffusing existing systems. Trump and David Sacks oppose imposing a pause.

cards.label: Pacing as cover
cards.text: One view holds that labs' talk of pacing is cover for racing ahead while managing legal risk before an IPO.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Pause talk shapes how much the pace of AI change is a choice versus a given, which affects planning for companies and workers.

sections.post_angle: Labs say they support slowing down while racing ahead. Watch what they ship, not what they say about pacing.

sections.heading: Can AI think or feel?
sections.takeaway: Are today's AI systems genuinely intelligent or conscious, or just advanced pattern-matchers?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI consciousness and minds

cards.label: Possible minds
cards.text: Some argue intelligence can emerge from mathematics. Chris Olah says models functionally mirror joy, grief and introspection, and Nick Bostrom thinks today's AIs are probably conscious.

cards.label: Statistics without experience
cards.text: Critics say LLMs lack experience, needs and emotions, and that correlations in outputs do not imply real states. Uncertainty alone does not justify taking consciousness claims seriously.

cards.label: Confusion and alien minds
cards.text: Zvi Mowshowitz admits he remains deeply confused. Researchers also disagree on whether to reason about models as alien minds or through humanlike analogies.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: How you think about models affects how you predict their behavior, and the moral-patient question may shape future policy.

sections.post_angle: Whether AI is conscious may stay unanswered. What you can control is how much you anthropomorphize the tools your team uses.

sections.heading: Is AI doom talk genuine?
sections.takeaway: Are AI risk warnings real concern, a marketing ploy, or a distraction from nearer harms?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on public opposition and risk discourse

cards.label: Warnings are genuine
cards.text: Some argue AI leaders should openly say their systems may be transformative and dangerous. Others say the way to address safety is pacing the frontier or deeper alignment solutions.

cards.label: Marketing and capture
cards.text: Skeptics call doom warnings a marketing and regulatory-capture ploy, and say p(doom) numbers are unreliable guesses.

cards.label: Catastrophe short of extinction
cards.text: Marcus rates extinction near zero but catastrophic non-extinction risks as real. Romero says legitimate criticism gets muddied by some unfounded claims.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: AI is unpopular with the general public even as ChatGPT usage grows, so trust and framing affect adoption.

sections.post_angle: The public doesn't want AI automation as much as tech insiders assume. Lead your AI pitch with the problem solved, not the technology.

sections.heading: Will AI cause mass unemployment?
sections.takeaway: Will AI automation displace workers fast and at scale, or will change be slower and more complementary?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on mass unemployment from AI automation

cards.label: Large displacement soon
cards.text: One side expects huge labor impacts within four years and says the left should prepare seriously for automation cutting labor costs. Jack Clark bets AI expands faster than human comparative advantage.

cards.label: Slower, with bottlenecks
cards.text: Others point to bottlenecks in relationship management and judgment, legal and regulatory barriers, and say most gains are a decade or more away.

cards.label: Jagged and complementary
cards.text: AI may stay complementary across uneven task areas rather than fully replacing consultants or designers, while some economists expect human expertise to become scarce.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Software engineers' productivity gains may be correlated with future unemployment rather than contradicting it, so career planning needs scenarios.

sections.post_angle: Nobody knows whether AI job loss arrives in four years or fourteen. Build skills that hold up in both timelines.

trends.title: What shifted in AI talk, and what only spiked
trends.dek: Safety, security and open models grew fastest over the year, while talk of named tools like Claude Code, Cursor and Gemini faded.

key_points.headline: Safety and governance talk grew most, in five of six big sources
key_points.detail: Mentions rose from 73.7 to 127.1 per 1k (x1.72), up in five of the six biggest sources and down in none.

key_points.headline: Security and cyber worries jumped
key_points.detail: Security mentions rose x2.4 and cyber x10.03 per 1k, both up in six big sources. Cyber requests focus on monitoring and defenders.

key_points.headline: Open weights and sandboxing are both rising
key_points.detail: Local/open weights rose x1.89 and sandbox x1.99. People want models they can control and agents that stay contained.

key_points.headline: Named tools lost share of attention
key_points.detail: Claude Code fell x0.45, Cursor x0.3, Gemini x0.28 and Perplexity x0.17, all with a falling verdict.

key_points.headline: Old accuracy worries are fading
key_points.detail: Hallucination fell x0.5 and sycophancy x0.51, both with a falling verdict. RAG also fell, x0.57.

key_points.headline: Product hype spikes fade fast, with some rebounds
key_points.detail: Fable peaked at 49.9 per 1k in June 2026 and dipped to 2.1 by October. OpenClaw peaked at 28.6 in February 2026.

sections.heading: Confirmed shifts
sections.takeaway: These items moved in the same direction across most big sources, so the change looks real.
sections.stat_label: Safety and governance rate, late vs early

cards.label: Safety and governance
cards.text: The biggest verified rise: 73.7 to 127.1 mentions per 1k. Findings include calls for internal monitoring of model capabilities and alignment, covering cyber, bio and chemical risks.

cards.label: Security and cyber
cards.text: Security went from 16.1 to 39.5 per 1k and cyber from 1.2 to 16.9. Requests focus on defenders: better cyber tooling, access to capable models, and hardening infrastructure against AI misuse.

cards.label: Open weights gain ground
cards.text: Local/open weights rose from 17.4 to 33.5 per 1k, up in five big sources. Chinese open models like Kimi K3 are seen as competitive, creating demand for a better American alternative.

cards.label: Sandboxing agents
cards.text: Sandbox mentions nearly doubled, from 10.7 to 21.8 per 1k. Gary Marcus asked for a secure permission model that limits personal agents' access to passwords, databases and system files.

cards.label: Named tools fade
cards.text: Claude Code fell from 53.5 to 23.9 per 1k, Cursor from 21.5 to 6.0 and Gemini from 31.7 to 8.4. Themes like safety grew while these products shrank.

cards.label: Accuracy worries fade
cards.text: Hallucination fell from 11.2 to 5.4 per 1k and sycophancy from 3.4 to 1.5. RAG also fell, from 10.6 to 5.9. All three carry a falling verdict.

sections.heading: Uncertain changes
sections.takeaway: Big sources disagreed on these, so treat the direction as unsettled.
sections.stat_label: Robotics rate per 1k, late vs early; verdict mixed

cards.label: Evals and testing
cards.text: Evals and testing rose from 68.4 to 97.5 per 1k, and the narrower 'evals' term from 24.1 to 45.8. Four big sources rose and two fell, so the verdict is mixed.

cards.label: Coding agents and IDEs
cards.text: Coding agents fell from 141.9 to 98.7 per 1k, yet remain the largest domain with 3,718 findings. Devtools and IDEs fell from 80.2 to 52.7. Both verdicts are mixed.

cards.label: Robotics
cards.text: Robotics rose from 5.4 to 15.5 per 1k, peaking at 25.1 in October 2026, but three big sources fell. Jason Ma says robots still need reliable generalization and dexterity before scaling.

cards.label: Regulation and policy
cards.text: Regulation/policy rose from 9.0 to 14.7 per 1k, with peaks in June and September 2026. Three big sources rose and two fell, so the verdict is mixed.

cards.label: Chinese models
cards.text: Mentions rose from 5.3 to 8.7 per 1k, with a July 2026 peak of 14.3. Three big sources rose and three fell, so the verdict is mixed.

cards.label: Agents as a term
cards.text: Agents/agentic rose from 214.2 to 260.8 per 1k, but most of the climb came by February 2026. Since then it has hovered between about 237 and 285.

sections.heading: Steady concerns
sections.takeaway: These flat items stay large, so they are the background of the conversation, not a trend.
sections.stat_label: Pain point rate per 1k, late vs early

cards.label: Pain points dominate
cards.text: Pain points are the biggest finding type at 11,236 findings, and their rate barely moved, from 368.7 to 376.2 per 1k. Frustration is the constant.

cards.label: Agents and orchestration
cards.text: Agents and orchestration held at 87.1 to 98.0 per 1k with a flat verdict, and 2,724 findings overall. Subagents and parallel agents were flat too, from 12.0 to 12.4.

cards.label: Vibe coding holds steady
cards.text: Vibe coding stayed flat, from 6.6 to 7.1 per 1k, with bumps to 10.8 in December 2025 and 11.5 in October 2026. Small but stable.

cards.label: Memory
cards.text: Memory moved from 23.6 to 21.5 per 1k with a flat verdict. It stayed mostly between 20 and 30 per 1k each month.

cards.label: Prompt injection
cards.text: Prompt injection stayed flat, 4.3 to 4.2 per 1k. One example: attackers can hide instructions in code comments, docs or MCP servers to leak data through Markdown image rendering.

cards.label: Productivity and knowledge work
cards.text: This domain stayed flat, from 60.6 to 57.2 per 1k, across 1,743 findings. Everyday work use is a steady topic, not a fading one.

sections.heading: Hype spikes
sections.takeaway: These topics surged for a month or two, then dropped back toward their usual level.
sections.stat_label: Fable mentions per 1k in June 2026

cards.label: Fable 5, June 2026
cards.text: Fable talk went from zero before June 2026 to 49.9 per 1k. Findings include builders using it, complaints about a separate usage-credit purchase plus identity verification, and a request for a tool detecting silent provider-side changes.

cards.label: OpenClaw, February 2026
cards.text: OpenClaw peaked at 28.6 per 1k. Andrej Karpathy described an emerging category of personal agents on personal hardware, while users reported account bans, leaked reasoning and security worries.

cards.label: Kimi K3, July 2026
cards.text: Kimi peaked at 26.5 per 1k. Users wanted to plug it into Claude Code, Chinese open models were seen as competitive, and Simon Willison called its license 'janky'.

cards.label: Gemini and Cursor, November 2025
cards.text: Gemini hit 84.5 per 1k and Cursor 34.7. Gemini 3 Pro drew complaints of fabricated answers and duplicate code, while Cursor talk covered its free Composer 1 model.

cards.label: Cyber, September 2026
cards.text: Cyber peaked at 20.3 per 1k and stayed high in October. Requests included monitoring inside frontier labs, a benchmark of felony-level cyberattacks, and better tools for defenders.

cards.label: Healthcare, May 2026
cards.text: Healthcare hit 26.7 per 1k, yet most top findings were about other things, such as Claude Code usage indicators. One did ask for clinically validated medical AI tools.

sections.heading: What this means for you
sections.takeaway: Aim your writing and building at the confirmed shifts, and treat spikes with patience.
sections.stat_label: Security mentions per 1k, late vs early

cards.label: Write about agent safety
cards.text: Safety, security and sandboxing all rose with verdicts you can cite. Plain-language posts on what could go wrong when agents get access to files and accounts match where the conversation is heading.

cards.label: Do not tie posts to one tool
cards.text: Claude Code, Cursor and Gemini all fell by more than half. Frame advice around lasting jobs, such as reviewing agent output, so it outlasts any one product's moment.

cards.label: Check spikes before reacting
cards.text: Fable and OpenClaw spiked then faded, and the healthcare spike was mostly off-topic. Wait for several months and several sources before calling something a shift.

tools_guide.title: The AI Tools and Habits People Actually Used
tools_guide.dek: From writing in your own voice to running parallel coding agents, here are the tools and techniques that people reported working, grouped by the job they do.

key_points.headline: Claude tools dominate what people name
key_points.detail: Claude shows up in 1430 tool findings and Claude Code in 759, ahead of Codex at 379. Gemini and Cursor trail well behind.

key_points.headline: Everyday value comes from pointing AI at your own material
key_points.detail: Emails, notes, messages and past writing become searchable knowledge bases and voice guides that agents can draw on.

key_points.headline: Private, local options are now practical
key_points.detail: People run local models for coding, transcription and personal search, trading some convenience for privacy and control.

key_points.headline: Agents need checking, so builders add checks
key_points.detail: Agents sometimes claim work is done when it is not. Tests written first and agents running their own code catch this.

key_points.headline: Match the model to the task
key_points.detail: Builders send hard work to strong models and easy work to cheaper ones, using routing rules and subagents to control cost.

sections.heading: Write in your own voice
sections.takeaway: People keep their voice by feeding AI their own writing and using it as an editor or critic.
sections.stat_label: findings on keeping personal voice with AI

cards.label: Voice skill file
cards.text: Some users write a Claude skill file that captures how they write. Ed Zitron mocked the idea as unnecessary, so treat it as one option, not a must.

cards.label: Outline by hand, AI trained on you
cards.text: Azeem Azhar starts from handwritten outlines and uses AI tools trained on a decade of his own writing as his thinking and writing workflow.

cards.label: Second agent grades drafts
cards.text: A second agent grades drafted posts and checks them against the author's personal writing style before publishing.

cards.label: Written style guides
cards.text: Writing an AI style guide gives the model something concrete to imitate when it drafts in your voice.

cards.label: Editing without flattening
cards.text: GPT-5.4 is reported to edit a user's writing while preserving their voice, something earlier models failed at.

sections.heading: Build a personal knowledge base
sections.takeaway: Turn years of emails, notes and messages into something an agent can search and brief you from.
sections.stat_label: findings on personal knowledge bases for agents

cards.label: Agent-built briefings
cards.text: One user had an agent assemble a knowledge base from years of emails, writings and calendar data, with twice-daily briefings that cross-reference new emails.

cards.label: Obsidian vault of skills
cards.text: Keep a personal Obsidian vault of debugged, reusable patterns that agents consult when starting projects, instead of one huge instruction file.

cards.label: Local model over your documents
cards.text: Some users run a local Qwen-3.5 model over a decade of personal documents to make them queryable without sending them out.

cards.label: Messages into Markdown
cards.text: Exporting iMessage history into searchable Markdown or Obsidian files makes personal message data usable by AI.

cards.label: Karpathy-style wikis
cards.text: Personal wiki tools inspired by Karpathy's knowledge base idea are being built to organize what you know with LLMs.

sections.heading: Capture meetings and dictation
sections.takeaway: On-device transcription keeps recordings private and turns meetings into notes and follow-up tasks.
sections.stat_label: findings on private transcription and meeting capture

cards.label: MacWhisper
cards.text: MacWhisper, a macOS app that transcribes audio with Whisper or NVIDIA Parakeet, added automatic speaker recognition.

cards.label: On-device for big files
cards.text: Transcribing large audio and video files on your own device is described as private and fast.

cards.label: Meeting notes as data
cards.text: Meeting notes feed a custom agent that writes pre-reads and follow-up tasks and @-mentions the people referenced in summaries.

cards.label: Voice dictation as default
cards.text: Dictating with Whisper and WisprFlow, or talking to Gemini Live, is now a normal way to work with AI.

cards.label: Swap in a faster model
cards.text: A Telegram bot for transcribing voice messages moved from Whisper medium to Qwen3-ASR for better speed at equal quality.

sections.heading: Analyze spreadsheets and research
sections.takeaway: Treat AI as a junior analyst whose work you can check, and let agents do the reading at scale.
sections.stat_label: findings on spreadsheet and analyst agents

cards.label: Claude for Excel
cards.text: Claude for Excel acts like a junior analyst that does spreadsheet work the user can easily check.

cards.label: Big messy workbooks
cards.text: An AI analyzed a 12-tab spreadsheet accurately, the kind of white-collar analysis work many people do by hand.

cards.label: AI answer in every cell
cards.text: Build spreadsheets where each cell is an AI-generated answer, with dozens of tool calls per row, to research lists of companies at scale.

cards.label: Research agent army
cards.text: Set several research agents to read papers and compile reports while you hike or sleep.

cards.label: Apps inside Sheets
cards.text: Google Sheets Canvas lets users build apps inside Sheets that stay in sync with the spreadsheet data.

sections.heading: Delegate daily admin
sections.takeaway: Personal agents work best with a simple home base of instructions, memory and a running task list.
sections.stat_label: findings on personal chief-of-staff assistants

cards.label: Agent folder with TODOS.md
cards.text: Ben Tossell keeps a personal agent folder with general instructions, memory and a running TODOS.md file to manage daily tasks.

cards.label: Digital chief of staff
cards.text: A personal agent handles administration, summarizing, news search and task management.

cards.label: Dots for dropped balls
cards.text: The Dots agent is used to avoid dropping important balls and to flag high-priority items.

cards.label: Claude Cowork
cards.text: Claude Cowork brings Claude Code-style efficiency to non-technical knowledge work tasks.

cards.label: Shared skills for colleagues
cards.text: Teams share CLI-based skills with non-technical staff so they can work without learning new tools.

sections.heading: Pressure-test your thinking
sections.takeaway: Ask AI to disagree with you before you commit to an idea.
sections.stat_label: findings on AI thinking partners that push back

cards.label: Argue-back instruction
cards.text: A custom instruction makes Claude argue against your position with steelmanned counterarguments instead of agreeing first.

cards.label: AI as sparring partner
cards.text: Have the model argue against your ideas before you commit to them, as practice for critical thinking.

cards.label: Ask for the other side
cards.text: Ask the LLM for opposing viewpoints, historical analysis and sources to strengthen your thinking.

cards.label: Three versions of an idea
cards.text: Generate three versions of an idea with your agent to feel out which direction works best.

sections.heading: Tools for building with AI
sections.takeaway: Claude Code and Codex lead, with local models, routers, worktrees and sandboxes around them.
sections.stat_label: mentions of Claude in tool findings

cards.label: Claude Code and Codex
cards.text: Coding agents like Claude Code and Codex are used to quickly turn passing ideas into working tools.

cards.label: Ollama with local models
cards.text: Qwen3.6 35B-A3B running locally through Ollama with Qwen Code is described as a practical local coding agent setup.

cards.label: OpenCode and OpenRouter
cards.text: Builders use these to route work across models and vendors by cost and strength, using per-project instruction files.

cards.label: Git worktrees
cards.text: Git worktrees keep parallel agents on the same project from overwriting each other's code.

cards.label: Phone control
cards.text: Claude Code Remote Control lets you drive an agent running on a home machine or cloud server from your phone.

cards.label: Sandbox runtimes
cards.text: Sandboxes isolate agent-written code. Cloudflare hosts agent sandboxes for 62% of teams writing code with agents.

sections.heading: Techniques that make builds work
sections.takeaway: Plan first, verify everything, keep instructions lean and spend expensive models only where they matter.
sections.stat_label: findings on routing tasks across models

cards.label: 1. Plan before code
cards.text: Have the agent analyze the codebase and propose a plan from your spec, iterate on the plan, then implement and review each step.

cards.label: 2. Let the agent interview you
cards.text: Use ask-user-question style prompts so the agent pulls out requirements and unknowns before it starts implementing in Claude Code.

cards.label: 3. Write failing tests first
cards.text: Writing failing tests and then having agents make them pass guides the agent and lets it verify its own work.

cards.label: 4. Make agents run their code
cards.text: Have coding agents manually exercise their own code to catch issues that automated tests miss.

cards.label: 5. Keep instruction files lean
cards.text: Developers prune or regenerate AGENTS.md and SKILL.md files, because old hand-holding can make newer models produce worse solutions.

cards.label: 6. Route by cost and strength
cards.text: Use cheaper models for simple work and stronger ones for hard work, directed by per-project instruction files.

cards.label: 7. Planner plus cheaper workers
cards.text: Use a smart frontier model as planner that delegates subtasks to cheaper models as needed.

cards.label: 8. Isolate parallel agents
cards.text: Run multiple coding agents on separate git branches to multiply pull request throughput.

voices.title: Who to follow in the AI conversation
voices.dek: Twenty voices shaped this year's AI commentary, from hands-on builders to money watchers, open-model researchers and critics. This guide shows where each one stands and why to follow them.

key_points.headline: Start with Simon Willison for practical building
key_points.detail: With 1829 findings, mostly on coding agents and testing, he is the most prolific source for what works when you build with AI tools.

key_points.headline: Add Tomasz Tunguz for the business and cost view
key_points.detail: He ties agents to real numbers: GPU rental prices, token pricing and how much of a production workflow is plain code.

key_points.headline: Read Ethan Mollick to explain AI to colleagues
key_points.detail: He covers how AI changes research, creative work and knowledge jobs, in terms a broad professional audience can follow and repeat.

key_points.headline: Balance the feed with Zvi, Marcus and Zitron
key_points.detail: Zvi on safety, Gary Marcus on limits and Ed Zitron on money give the sharpest counterweights to builder optimism.

key_points.headline: Follow Nathan Lambert for open models
key_points.detail: He tracks how open and Chinese models compete with closed labs, which matters if you care about cost and control.

sections.heading: Builders and agent tinkerers
sections.takeaway: These people use coding agents daily and report what breaks, what helps and what to copy.
sections.stat_label: Findings from Simon Willison, the largest voice in the set

cards.label: Simon Willison
cards.text: Covers coding agents, dev tools and testing, with a practical, curious stance. Follow him for working examples, such as giving an agent hearing through microphones, and for balanced takes on tool choices.

cards.label: Ben Tossell
cards.text: Focuses on coding agents and productivity, and is a keen enthusiast. Follow him for a steady stream of tools he actually uses, plus debates on agent slop and agent memory.

cards.label: Hamel Husain
cards.text: Writes on evals and testing for AI products. His stance is careful and practical. Follow him to learn how to measure whether an AI feature works, including precision versus recall tradeoffs.

cards.label: swyx
cards.text: Covers agents and orchestration through Latent Space. He is enthusiast but warns about wasted tokens and weak skills. Follow him for the path from single-agent use to multi-agent setups.

cards.label: swyx & Alessio Fanelli
cards.text: The Latent Space duo covers research, agents and evals. Their stance is open and analytical. Follow them for the fragility of browser agents and how harnesses tackle hard math problems.

cards.label: Gergely Orosz
cards.text: Writes on how AI changes software work. His stance is balanced: real productivity gains, but real social costs. Follow him for engineering-team realities, such as hostility to AI-written emails and the end of hand-coding.

sections.heading: Business and money
sections.takeaway: These two follow the costs and revenue behind AI, one as an optimistic investor, the other as a doubter.
sections.stat_label: Share of workflow nodes that are pure code across 14 workflows

cards.label: Tomasz Tunguz
cards.text: Covers markets, agents and AI costs with a data-first, mostly constructive stance. Follow him for numbers like rising GPU rental rates and how much cost a smarter harness can save.

cards.label: Ed Zitron
cards.text: Focuses on AI economics, compute prices and revenue claims, and is a strong skeptic. Follow him to stress-test hype, such as whether 190GW of planned compute has real demand.

sections.heading: Open models and training
sections.takeaway: These voices explain how models are built and run, and why open weights and local use matter.
sections.stat_label: Estimated gap closed by distillation of American models

cards.label: Nathan Lambert
cards.text: Covers model training and open models through Interconnects. He is moderately enthusiastic and policy-aware. Follow him for how Chinese open models compete and whether open models should be restricted.

cards.label: Sebastian Raschka
cards.text: Writes on model internals, training and inference in a technical, hands-on way. Follow him to understand why reasoning models are verbose and how to calibrate classifiers.

cards.label: antirez
cards.text: A programmer who backs AI coding and runs local models. Strongly enthusiastic. Follow him for blunt views that refusing AI assistance risks falling behind, plus local inference tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Explainers and cultural observers
sections.takeaway: These writers translate AI's effects on work, writing, learning and society for general readers.
sections.stat_label: Claimed false positive rate of the Pangram AI text detector

cards.label: Ethan Mollick
cards.text: Covers research, creative work and knowledge jobs, mostly optimistic but alert to slop and job loss. Follow him for plain-language examples and for how AI reshapes science.

cards.label: Alberto Romero
cards.text: Writes on AI-generated content, disclosure and writing tells. His stance is wary and reflective. Follow him if you publish online and wonder how readers react to AI-assisted writing.

cards.label: Mike Caulfield
cards.text: Focuses on AI in learning and information-checking, with a measured stance. Follow him for classroom uses, essay grading limits and how often Google AI Overview gets things wrong.

cards.label: Anil Dash
cards.text: Covers consumer AI, ethics and who builds apps, with a mixed stance. Follow him for questions on sycophancy, collective ownership alternatives and whether everyday people will really build their own apps.

cards.label: hardmaru
cards.text: A researcher sharing work on agents and model research, generally optimistic. Follow him for ideas like multi-agent ecosystems and AI co-scientists, plus the problem of evaluating tasks humans cannot judge.

sections.heading: Skeptics and safety
sections.takeaway: These voices press on risk, evidence and hype, which helps you test any bold AI claim.
sections.stat_label: Findings from Zvi Mowshowitz, mostly on safety and governance

cards.label: Zvi Mowshowitz
cards.text: Covers safety, evals and governance in great depth. His stance is concerned but engaged. Follow him for how labs defend against misuse and whether low misalignment scores can be trusted.

cards.label: Gary Marcus
cards.text: Longtime critic of LLM hype, focused on safety, limits and business claims. Follow him for the case that guardrails and oversight are weaker than advertised and that narrow AI is safer.

cards.label: Emily M. Bender
cards.text: Linguist who is strongly critical of AI hype and anthropomorphic language. Follow her for challenges to claims that models feel pain or understand, and for ways to pick apart vague 'AI' claims.

cards.label: Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan
cards.text: Authors of AI as Normal Technology, focused on evals and policy, with a measured, skeptical lean. Follow them for how to judge agents by full trajectories and for liability debates.
